newsitem.title: USA: U.S. zinc stockpile sales spat set to continue.
newsitem.headline: U.S. zinc stockpile sales spat set to continue.

text.p: The row between U.S. producer lobby, the American Zinc Association, and the government over how much stockpiled zinc should be sold remained unresolved as the latter appeared to step up its sales effort.
The AZA argued that the effect of stockpile sales should be measured against the market for the specific grades sold rather than the much larger overall zinc market.
The stockpile has authority to sell 50,000 short tons of prime western and high grade metal in fiscal 1997. The bulk of the U.S. market of 1.3 million tons is special high grade.
The General Accounting Office issued a 50-page report late last week concluding that the stockpile's sales criteria was right all along.
The U.S. has to import some two-thirds of its zinc needs.

"We believe the government's determination has a sound basis," the GAO report said. "It is based on practices that exist in the zinc industry, and it is consistent with the views of zinc market participants with whom we discussed this matter."

AZA executive director George Vary said the report gave a green light to the stockpile to offer 7,500 short tons of zinc each month instead of the 4,000 short tons offered before the GAO released its report.
The maximum the stockpile can sell is still 50,000 tons, in fiscal 1997 which began October 1, but Vary believed the stockpile will in future sell its metal more aggressively.
"Now the GAO has taken the clamps off them, they are going to sell up to the maximum," Vary said.
GAO and Defense National Stockpile Center officials were not immediately available for comment. Monday is a federal holiday to observe Veterans Day.
Nevertheless, Vary said the GAO and AZA have agreed on the size of the U.S. PW and HG zinc market at 250,000 short tons.
Congress will now consider the GAO's report but it was not clear if there will be any hearings as mentioned when the GAO was asked by Rep Herbert Bateman in October last year to look into zinc sales.
"I hope somebody will say 250,000 tons is the market and 50,000 tons of annual sales sounds high," Vary said.
Annual stockpile sales of 25,000 short tons or about 10 percent of the PW and HG markets would be more in line, he added.
The AZA argued that the effect of stockpile zinc sales should be measured against part rather than the whole of the U.S. market because the different grades of metal are not interchangeable.
"Steel mills cannot use high grade or prime western metal," Vary said. The GAO disagreed.

Vary said the GAO report was contradictory when it stated "We did not conclude that zinc itself is fungible in all, or even most, uses, at least not given the range of price differences in the market."

But elsewhere in the report the GAO added, "In any event, the government's determination of undue disruption of the usual market does not depend on the specific size of the high grade and prime western market alone, but rather on the larger market for all grades of zinc."
U.S. government stockpile sales of zinc have attracted complaints from foreign producer countries.
-- Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646
